title: Applying AI to Global Food Insecurity: ZeroHungerAI
transcriptText:
We now find ourselves at an inflection
point where the challenges to food
security are at once growing in their
scope and complexity while at the same
time AI and AI-enabled technologies
promise improved and novel solutions to
create more resilient, more prosperous
global food systems.
To help bring this promise to fruition,
Google.org has launched the AI
Collaborative Food Security
which connects organizations working at
the forefront of AI-enabled food
security solutions. As part of our
first-ever AI for Food Security Forum,
we'll hear from several of them here
today. I'm Zane Swanson, Deputy Director
and Fellow with the Global Food and
Water Security Program here at CSIS. It
is my pleasure to be joined by Philip
Zimmer,
Zero Hunger AI Project Lead at World
Bank Group's dime AI, as we examine how
they are using and implementing
AI-enabled tools to improve early
warning systems for food security.
Philip, thank you very much for joining
us today. Thank you, Zane.
So,
early warning systems, people think of
them in a lot of different ways, but not
always for food security.
Tell me why early warning systems are
important for food security and why you
at World Bank are thinking about it that
way. Yeah, thank you so much, Zane. So,
this comes very much back to a simple
promise that uh
in humanitarian response and also in
development programming, very often the
way we operate still today is that we
don't really have an early detection of
crises and this unfortunately then leads
to very delayed responses, both on the
humanitarian side, but also with
development programming being very much
reactive to emerging trends in society.
And this is often then contributing to
high loss of life and also high
humanitarian costs when it comes to
responding to crises.
So, the idea behind food insecurity
forecasting and forecasting more broadly
speaking is really to create a proactive
and anticipatory environment. So, what
we really care about is capturing early
warning signals and that can, you You
the case of food insecurity, be around
conflict, around agriculture, around
climate shocks. But, you can also
extrapolate this idea to different
thematic areas, whether it is generally
about anticipating conflict, health
outcomes, disease outbreaks, et cetera.
So, if we're able to capture these early
warning signals, the idea is that that
we can inform anticipatory action. So,
acting in anticipation of the crisis,
not necessarily to prevent the crisis.
Some crises will not be able to be
prevented, but at least to do a better
the effects of these crises on lives and
livelihoods around the globe.
So, early warning systems for food
security and and lots of other forms of
human security have existed for a long
time. You guys are doing something
really interesting leveraging AI to
improve those and actually have novel
tools. So, tell us a little bit about
how you're doing that today. Yeah,
thanks for the question, Zane. So, as
you mentioned, there's a lot of exciting
initiatives out there already, but
something we see consistently a
challenge across the space, and you
know, this doesn't only apply about food
security, but also other thematic areas
in development and humanitarian action,
is that data gaps still prevent these
powerful models that we're building and
trying to train these days to have
really their real show their real
promise and their real impact. So, a few
years ago, we started under the idea,
the hypothesis that we can maybe get
proxy signal on the very known risk
factors and risk drivers of food crises
across conflict, agriculture, climate
shocks, economic crises, et cetera. So,
we are testing the hypothesis that news
reporting, particularly local news
reporting, will be able to uncover a lot
of these dynamics that we observe and
that we know contribute to food crises
earlier than the traditional indicators.
So, what we're doing is in the end of
the day very simple. We look into news
reporting both on a global and at the
local level, and then we extract and
track the different known risk factors
across the different thematic areas.
What we then do is take the signal from
the raw news articles and turn it into
structured data. The high frequency
signal that we know can provide us
pretty good insights up until the
district level to then feed this into
our forecasting models, but also as a
data source itself. Because what we've
observed in conversations with our
operational colleagues, but also
partners in the new humanitarian space,
the very often decision makers
yes, they care about the famous red dot
on the map, but they also want to know
what is driving the crisis. Because the
response if you're on operations in in
the World Bank will be very different if
food insecurity is driven by climate
shocks or whether it is driven by
overall climate change and therefore the
need for more climate resilient seeds
and and crops. So, this is the type of
interpretable signal that we also can
harness with the news. I think you have
some really interesting results to to
point at. So, can you talk us through
some of those? Yeah, so what we did here
was doing an evaluation of our approach
across 21 countries where we have human
ground truth data on this field on food
insecurity. And the common indicator
that's being used here is the IPC phase,
which is a consortium based consensus
based
expert group. And so, what we try to
compare here is to which extent human
expert forecasts compared to traditional
models, traditional models essentially
meaning using these traditional signals
like
fatality counts, rainfall levels, etc.
But then also what happens if we add
this additional signal from the news
that I was talking about.
So, we compare here the ability of these
models to predict food crisis outbreaks,
often times defined as the IPC phase
reaching three or higher.
And the first observation is that if we
use traditional machine learning
approaches and traditional signal, these
often times often outperform human
experts.
The first good promise of that we can
really leverage machine learning and AI
here.
Second and more interesting is that if
we feed news by themselves as an own
signal, but also in combination and
that's probably even more exciting, with
traditional signal, um we can do a much
much better job at anticipating of food
crisis outcomes. And we see in in the
study across 21 countries that more than
46% uh the 46% more food crisis
outbreaks were able to detect. Um and
this really spans different geographies,
different types of crises, and different
drivers of of crises. Um so really
exciting uh approach for this field.
And let's dig down on that a little bit.
So if we're thinking about different
geographies, let's think about instances
where these models could have been
really uh useful. Yeah, so we have two
examples we've brought here just to also
illustrate of
our understanding of why we think
working with the news helps, right?
Intuitively, that's maybe a funny idea,
an interesting approach, but you know,
operationally, what is really happening
here? And
there's first a case from the Mayendit
district in South Sudan where an IPC
phase 3 was declared in 2017.
And what we saw that a few weeks
earlier, one of the common traditional
indicators, the vegetation index, was
deteriorating significantly. So
essentially,
what was happening to the fields and the
and the farms was eventually in food
production was eventually influencing uh
food security in the region. Now
interestingly enough, already months
earlier the we see in the news that
there were significant spikes in
conversations around crop diseases and
pest outbreaks.
So what was essentially happening was
that local farmers were observing new
bugs in their fields, and they were
getting very concerned about the
upcoming harvest. And so this chatter
was what local journalists were picking
up on and reporting on. And this is
exactly what we were able to extract
here when monitoring the news, much
earlier than what when the outcomes were
observed in geospatial data.
So crop pests are a huge uh
stressor on agricultural systems around
the world, but what's actually driving
the most food insecurity in the world
right now is conflict. So you can also
track that, right? Yes. So there's a
case from from Somalia um and here we
had a
IPC phase four declared in 2011. And
what we saw was that essentially this
food crisis was largely driven by
violence and and conflict. But some of
the traditional indicators that formally
record fatalities of of violence and of
conflicts were actually not catching up
with what was happening on the ground.
So, there were not yet any official
records of fatalities while a few months
earlier we observed again spikes in the
news on
on violent events. And so, what these
two examples just out of of many cases
illustrate is that the news can help us
both get signal earlier than traditional
indicators, but also sometimes uncover
some uncover some of these blind spots
that unfortunately still exist today.
So, these are both really great examples
and I think two really great examples
about two different ways that AI is
really improving
early warning systems. First, creating
novel tools, but then also enabling the
the greater system of early warning if
you combine those tools into existing
modes.
Talk a little bit about that. Yeah,
thanks so much Zain and this is also
what we're super excited with our
project to be part of the collaborative.
So, as you saw in one of the previous
slides where I was highlighting the the
different performances of the different
models is that ultimately what we're
aiming for is not so much to replace all
the traditional data, but to really use
the news as a supplement to this
exciting space that already exists. So,
there's all these different initiatives,
you know, that are trying to capture and
understand different risk drivers of
food crises. And our idea is to really
bring these together in a central place
that can serve as a bird's-eye view to
this topic and then supplement this
ecosystem with the signal from the news
that we're currently
tracking across 82 countries at the
district level.
And we can see some of that tracking
here. Yeah, wonderful. So, what we're
building is also a publicly accessible
platform where users will both be able
to visualize the data directly. This is
particularly tailored to decision makers
at the World Bank, but also outside. But
then other partners in the space will
also be able to access that data. And to
really get the insights of a more than
140 million articles from almost 100,000
sources that we're currently tracking.
And what's very exciting as we think
also about the integration of this work
into operations and decision making is
that when users interact with the app,
they will not be only able to see
forecasts of food crisis up to 12 months
in advance, but they will also be able
to drill down into what we're observing
in our data and particularly in the news
reporting. Where we see oscillations in
different dimensions of crises, whether
there's conflict in this chatter around,
you know, violent events that we're
picking up on and that our model sees is
driving this crisis, or whether there's
maybe an observations around
agricultural events and or climate
shocks.
Now, operationally speaking, who is
actually the one using this? Um and so
first and foremost within our own
organization at the World Bank, we're
very actively currently thinking about
how this will be supplement to the
crisis response window, one of the main
crisis financing arms and organizations
in in the World Bank, but we're also
thinking about how this will be expanded
towards other organizations, whether
it's the surf fund it at the UN, but
also as operational insights for
colleagues at WFP that we're working
with very closely.
Wonderful. Well, thank you for all of
this. I think the work that you're doing
at Zero Hunger AI is obviously important
for early warning systems and food
security generally, but is a really
important part of a greater whole, which
is how we use AI and leverage the sort
of innovation that it produces
to actually move the needle on the
ground for those that need it the most.
Thank you, Philip. Thanks for joining
us. Thank you, Zane.
